docs.title: Migration from immunarch v0.9 to v1.0
docs.text:
This guide is for existing immunarch users. If you're new to immunarch, you can safely skip this tutorial.

Note: The 0.9.y versions of immunarch (e.g., 0.9.1) are no longer supported. If something breaks (e.g., due to a dependency update), it will not be fixed. I highly recommend upgrading to version 0.10 as soon as possible. Version 0.10 serves as a pre-release version for 1.0, and feature parity between 0.9 and 1.0 will be achieved within a few months. Once it is done, the version 0.10.x will be switched to 1.0.

I'm prioritizing feature parity, stability, and enhancements for the most common workflows as well as advanced use cases relevant to immunotherapy development. If you need help with migration or run into issues, please open an issue on GitHub - I'm happy to help.

docs.title: High-level overview of v1.0 changes
docs.text: Version 1.0 introduces several important changes compared to the 0.9.x series.

docs.title: 1) Working with data
docs.text:
Version 1.0 embraces a much clearer data layer centered on ImmunData from immundata R package. ImmunData is a lightweight, consistent data structure for working with chains, receptors, and repertoires. It promotes immutability, i.e., functions no longer mutate your data in place, but instead return new objects. This makes pipelines easier to reason about and eliminates hidden side effects, but requires changes in how you think about the data analysis. Read more in the Concepts section.

ImmunData is designed to be scale-agnostic. Today, you can use small immune repertoire samples; tomorrow, you can plug in larger-than-memory datasets with zero changes to your code. The API remains stable and your analysis code stays simple.

docs.title: 2) API changes
docs.text:
Some function signatures have changed. Large, multi-tool functions are now split into smaller, focused ones.

Example: The old repDiversity() meta-function is now a family of functions, each with a clear, shared prefix. For instance, you now call airr_diversity_shannon() or airr_diversity_pielou(). These functions are still grouped under one help page so you can compare them and discover new metrics easily. Simply run ?airr_diversity to get a list of all functions in the family. This holds for virtually all other function families - ?airr_stats, ?airr_clonality, ?annotate_clonality, etc.

You'll find smaller, clearer tools with consistent naming and arguments throughout. The reason is that with huge multi-tool functions such as repOverlap it requires a lot of cognitive investment to remember specific method arguments. With smaller function you can effortlessly invoke a help from IDE itself via autocomplete by pressing "tab" while typing the function name.

  • Watch for deprecations. If the console says "deprecated" or "will be removed in v1.1.0", please update your code soon. Compatibility shims are temporary and will eventually be removed.

docs.title: 3) Fewer heavy dependencies
docs.text: Many packages were moved from Depends to Suggests. As a result, immunarch now installs much faster and brings in far fewer dependencies. The 0.9 version would pull in around 140 packages on a clean machine, while 0.10 is closer to 80. If you use a feature that requires an optional package, you'll see a clear prompt telling you what to install.

docs.title: 4) Working with visualizations
docs.text:
The vis() function family has not been implemented for the new analysis functions – yet. This was a deliberate choice. The major downside of vis() lies in its general nature: sadly, one-size-fits-all didn't work as expected. Programmatically producing publication-ready plots is extremely challenging, and most users end up editing the generated plots to fit journal requirements anyway. For examples of what's involved in preparing plots to publication, see this guide to publication-ready ggplot2.

Currently, I provide ggplot2 code templates for common publication figures in the tutorials and guides. This approach not only helps you learn ggplot2 (the standard for scientific plotting in R), but also ensures your figures match your desired style or journal specifications right from the start.

My plan is to update vis() to support 1.0 analysis methods. Run ?vis() to check if something changed and there is no "deprecated" flag. However, the new implementation strategy will be completely different: opinionated and lightweight visualisations in 1.0 instead of heavy and general solutions for all possible use cases in 0.9. In other words, new vis() won't be able to produce all kinds of plots. The created plots will serve the major purpose of helping you quickly understand your data, rather than providing all the tweaks and gears for publication-ready plots. And if you want to change something, please use ggplot2 and read that great guide on publication-ready plots.

  • Where can I find themes and palettes? Check out ggsci and this curated palette list for easy, beautiful color options.

To view the latest migration updates, run get_immunarch_news() in your R console.

docs.title: If you must stay on immunarch v0.9
docs.text:
If you absolutely must freeze the last stable version before 1.0, use one of the following installation methods:

  • pak:

pak::pkg_install("immunarch@=0.9.1")
* install.packages:

install.packages("https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/immunarch/immunarch_0.9.1.tar.gz", repos = NULL, type = "source")
* conda:

mamba install -c conda-forge r-immunarch=0.9.1

Reminder: 0.9.x will receive no further updates or fixes.

docs.title: Why do I even need 1.0?
docs.text:
• Outdated code is hard to maintain, especially in academic environments where developer turnover is high. New immunarch code is much easier to support and remember what it does.
  • Improved code culture: modern best practices, standard data structures, consistent naming, and more - all of this in the new ecosystem of tools, where immunarch is the core.
  • Lazy backends for large-scale data: thanks to amazing people behind DuckDB, duckplyr, Arrow and Parquet, immunarch now supports out-of-memory datasets without any code changes on your side.
  • Parallelization: where possible, immunarch steps will run in parallel out of the box, speeding up your analyses, efficiently using modern server architecture.

Stay tuned for updates in 2025. If you have questions or migration issues, please reach out on GitHub. Thank you!

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This vignette is a practical, end‑to‑end guide to analyzing single‑chain and paired‑chain Adaptive Immune Receptor Repertoire (AIRR) data derived from single‑cell assays (scRNA‑seq with VDJ, also often referred to as scVDJ‑seq / scTCR‑seq / scBCR‑seq). It starts from the basics and builds up to more advanced analyses, so it can serve both as a first stop for newcomers and as a focused introduction to specific topics for experienced readers.

docs.title: What you'll learn
docs.text:
• Load single‑cell V(D)J data and sample metadata into immunarch.
  • Define receptors (AA vs NT), set chain‑pairing rules, and perform essential QC.
  • Define repertoires.
  • Explore repertoire features: expansion, gene usage, CDR3 properties, and diversity.
  • Quantify overlap/similarity between samples and conditions.
  • Discover public receptors and their statistics.
  • Link receptors to single‑cell transcriptomic clusters for downstream interpretation.

docs.title: Dataset used in this tutorial
docs.text:
We will work with data for patient 6 from the study "Peripheral T cell expansion predicts tumour infiltration and clinical response" (Wu et al.; Nature 579:274--278, 2020). The dataset includes three compartments per patient: tumour, peripheral blood, and normal adjacent tissue (NAT). We will demonstrate a typical single‑cell AIRR workflow across these three samples. Here are the main findings of the study:

  • Deep single‑cell RNA/TCR profiling across tumour, NAT, and blood
  • Clonotypic expansion of effector‑like T cells in and around tumours
  • Patients with stronger peripheral expansion signatures tend to respond better to anti‑PD‑(L)1 therapy
  • Expanded intratumoural clonotypes are often detectable in blood, enabling convenient monitoring

References & data access:

  • Wu TD, Madireddi S, de Almeida PE, et al. Nature (2020). "Peripheral T cell expansion predicts tumour infiltration and clinical response."
  • GEO series: GSE139555 (single‑cell RNA/TCR; pretreatment samples from 14 patients; tumour/NAT/blood).

docs.title: Typical workflow: from files to analysis
docs.text:
Analysing single-cell AIRR data with immunarch and immundata follows a reproducible workflow that separates data ingestion from downstream transformation and annotation. Sounds scary, but in reality it is a rather straightforward approach: load and preprocess the data first, and analyse it second - instead of having steps mixed in an arbitrary order. This separation lets you reanalyse large datasets without repeatedly reading and preprocessing the original receptor files.

The workflow is divided into two phases.

  1. Ingestion phase

    • Read the manifest file with immune repertoire metadata (optional but recommended)
    • Define receptors using a schema (e.g., single or paired chains, custom features)
    • Optionally define a repertoire schema (to compare repertoire-level statistics such as diversity)
    • Load AIRR-seq files from disk
    • Process the input files and store the dataset as an immutable, on-disk ImmunData object.

  2. Transformation phase

    • Annotate ImmunData with external information (e.g., scRNA-seq clusters, immunogenicity information)
    • Regroup repertoires on the fly (e.g., by tissue, donor, or cell state) to better reflect the biomarkers you are looking for
    • Filter, mutate, and compute statistics
    • Visualize results, save plots, or export annotations back to Seurat/AnnData

You can read more about the phases in Concepts → Ingestion Phase.

docs.title: Note: materialization
docs.text:
Tip: Use materialization for final summaries, plots, or tables, but keep your core ImmunData object on disk and in its lazy, efficient format for most analyses.

The ImmunData object from immundata is designed to handle large, out-of-memory datasets efficiently. Instead of loading everything into RAM, it stores computations and only runs them when the results are actually needed, e.g., for plotting or summarizing data. This is called lazy evaluation.

Materialization means executing all pending computations and bringing the results into memory as a concrete table or data frame. This approach is powerful for working with large datasets, but can be unfamiliar if you're used to working entirely in-memory.

If you see an error like:

Error: Materialization is disabled, use collect() or as_tibble() to materialize.

...it means your data hasn't been materialized yet (i.e., the computation hasn't run and the results aren't present in R memory).

  • For small results (e.g., summary stats, small tables), simply call collect() or as_tibble() at the end of your pipeline to materialize the data:
result <- some_immunarch_function(idata) |> collect()
  • For large datasets (e.g., a fully filtered ImmunData object), avoid materializing unless you're sure you need all data in memory --- this could use significant RAM and slow down your workflow.

You can read more about materialization in Concepts → Immutability.

Next, get the file paths to the V(D)J data packaged with immundata:

R 
inp_files <- paste0(system.file("extdata/single_cell", "", package = "immundata"), "/*.csv.gz")

What is a "receptor" from a data analysis perspective? A receptor is the central unit of analysis and is defined by:

  • The features used for grouping (e.g., cdr3, v_call, j_call)
  • The chains involved (e.g., TRB for TCR beta, or paired TRA+TRB)

Defining a receptor schema lets you flexibly group TCR/BCR sequences for downstream analysis and compute statistics on them.

Here's how to define a basic single-chain receptor schema: TRB chains, grouped by both cdr3 and v_call (amino acid sequence and V gene).

R 
schema <- make_receptor_schema(features = c("cdr3", "v_call"), chains = c("TRB"))

If you want to use other receptor definitions, you can create and pass custom schemas to read_repertoires(). Below are a few examples:

# Paired-chain

# The strictest receptor definition

[1] "cdr3"   "v_call" "j_call"

$chains
[1] "TRA" "TRB"

The main entry point for loading AIRR-seq data into the immunarch framework is the read_repertoires() function from immundata. This function handles everything from reading raw files, to preprocessing and aggregation, to joining sample metadata and saving an efficient on-disk ImmunData object for reproducible analysis.

The key parameters you'll want to understand:

  • path: vector of input file paths, e.g., to AIRR TSV, 10X CSV, or Parquet files. (You can use Sys.glob() to collect files.)
  • schema: defines how receptors are grouped; typically created with make_receptor_schema().
  • manifest: optional data frame with sample-level metadata, read by read_manifest().
  • barcode_col: name of the column containing cell barcodes (e.g., "barcode" for 10x single-cell data); this triggers single-cell logic.
  • locus_col: name of the column specifying the chain (e.g., "locus" for TRA/TRB distinction).
  • umi_col: column for UMI counts (e.g., "umis"); used to select dominant chains per barcode.
  • preprocess: list of preprocessing steps to apply before aggregation. The preset make_default_preprocessing("10x") works for standard 10x data.
  • repertoire_schema: columns in metadata (or annotation) used to define repertoires (e.g., "Tissue" to split by compartment).

Here's how to use it on the packaged single-cell demo dataset:

schema <- make_receptor_schema(features = c("cdr3", "v_call"), chains = c("TRB"))

idata <- read_repertoires(path = inp_files,

To visualize gene expression and link it with immune repertoires, load the expression matrix into a Seurat object. Here, we use a cached RDS to speed up the tutorial:

R 
url <- "https://zenodo.org/records/15604205/files/l6data.rds?download=1"
dest <- BiocFileCache::bfcrpath(BiocFileCache::BiocFileCache(ask = FALSE), url)

mat <- readr::read_rds(dest)

sdata <- CreateSeuratObject(counts = mat)

embeddings <- as.matrix(cells[c("UMAP_1", "UMAP_2")])
rownames(embeddings) <- cells$barcode

umap_dr <- CreateDimReducObject(embeddings = embeddings, key = "UMAP_", assay = DefaultAssay(sdata))

sdata[["umap"]] <- umap_dr

Idents(sdata) <- setNames(cells$ident, cells$barcode)

DimPlot(sdata, reduction = "umap", order = sort(unique(cells$ident), decreasing = TRUE), label = TRUE, alpha = .5)

docs.title: How to read other types of data --- bulk, single-chain, etc.
docs.text:
The read_repertoires() function is flexible and supports many repertoire data types and formats. Here are practical patterns for different scenarios. Use these examples as templates to adapt to your own data sources and formats.

Note: These code blocks are for demonstration and not intended to run as part of this tutorial. The "Tissue" column must be present in your data if you want to define repertoires by tissue.

docs.title: 1. Bulk sequencing
docs.text:
For bulk AIRR-seq data, you generally don't need barcode_col, locus_col, or umi_col. Optionally provide count_col if your data includes receptor counts.

R 
idata <- read_repertoires(path = inp_files, 
                          schema = schema, 
                          manifest = manifest, 
                          count_col = "counts", 
                          preprocess = make_default_preprocessing("airr"), 
                          repertoire_schema = "Tissue")

docs.title: 2. Single-cell sequencing
docs.text:
For single-cell data, you'll typically need all columns (barcode, locus, UMI) for proper chain aggregation and cell assignment.

R 
idata <- read_repertoires(path = inp_files, 
                          schema = schema, 
                          manifest = manifest, 
                          barcode_col = "barcode", 
                          locus_col = "chain", 
                          umi_col = "umis", 
                          preprocess = make_default_preprocessing("10x"), 
                          repertoire_schema = "Tissue")

docs.title: 3. AIRR-C or 10x Genomics format
docs.text:
Both AIRR-C and 10x Genomics formats are supported. Pay attention to the receptor schema, locus column (locus or chain), and use the correct preset for make_default_preprocessing().

R 
#
# AIRR-C
#
schema <- make_receptor_schema(features = c("junction_aa", "v_call"), chains = "TCRB")
# or
schema <- make_receptor_schema(features = c("cdr3_aa", "v_call"), chains = "TCRB")
# reminder how to read paired-chain data if needed:
schema <- make_receptor_schema(features = c("cdr3_aa", "v_call"), chains = c("TCRA", "TCRB"))

idata <- read_repertoires(path = inp_files, 
                          schema = schema, 
                          manifest = manifest,
                          barcode_col = "cell_id",
                          locus_col = "locus",
                          umi_col = "umi_count", 
                          preprocess = make_default_preprocessing("airr"), 
                          repertoire_schema = "Tissue")

#
# 10XGenomics
#

# This is how the original schema would look like
schema <- make_receptor_schema(features = c("cdr3_aa", "v_gene"), chains = "TRB")

idata <- read_repertoires(path = inp_files, 
                          schema = schema, 
                          manifest = manifest, 
                          barcode_col = "barcode", 
                          locus_col = "chain", 
                          umi_col = "umis", 
                          preprocess = make_default_preprocessing("10x"),
                          rename_columns = NULL,
                          repertoire_schema = "Tissue")

# Immundata renames some columns by default to match them with AIRR-C format.
# So we use this:
schema <- make_receptor_schema(features = c("cdr3", "v_call"), chains = "TRB")

idata <- read_repertoires(path = inp_files, 
                          schema = schema, 
                          manifest = manifest, 
                          barcode_col = "barcode", 
                          locus_col = "locus", 
                          umi_col = "umis", 
                          preprocess = make_default_preprocessing("10x"),
                          repertoire_schema = "Tissue")

docs.title: 4. Reading file paths from manifest
docs.text:
If your manifest contains file paths, you can use the special path = "<manifest>" argument. Specify which column in your manifest has the file paths with manifest_file_col.

R 
idata <- read_repertoires(path = "<manifest>", 
                          schema = schema, 
                          manifest = manifest, 
                          barcode_col = "barcode", 
                          locus_col = "locus",
                          umi_col = "umis", 
                          preprocess = make_default_preprocessing("10x"),
                          repertoire_schema = "Tissue")

docs.title: Key immune repertoire statistics
docs.text:
A well-designed immune repertoire analysis always starts with a set of basic descriptive statistics. These help you:

  • Check data quality (e.g., are all samples/cell types well-represented?)
  • Spot technical artifacts (e.g., biased V gene usage, length skews)
  • Summarize diversity and composition for downstream biological or clinical questions

The immunarch package provides a family of functions, airr_desc_*, to quickly compute these statistics from your ImmunData object. To see all options or details, run ?airr_desc in your R console.

Currently there are three functions to compute key statistics:

  1. airr_desc_chains() counts the number of chains (e.g., TRA, TRB, IGH units) and unique receptors per repertoire/sample. Use this for library size, capture depth, and to check chain balance (e.g., are you missing TRA?).

  2. airr_desc_lengths() summarizes the CDR3 length distribution per repertoire. Reveals if your data has technical biases, primer effects, or biologically meaningful skews (like more long or short clones in a disease).

  3. airr_desc_genes() counts the usage of V, D, or J genes per repertoire/sample/cluster. Essential for characterizing repertoire composition, comparing patient groups, or making features for ML models.

docs.title: 1a. Number of receptors and barcodes for samples
docs.text:
Let's start by quantifying two basic properties:

  • Number of unique barcodes per sample (reflects cell yield)

  • Number of unique receptors per sample (reflects immune diversity)

These metrics are often used as a first-line QC and as a way to detect outliers or sample-specific technical effects. Large differences in barcode count may indicate sample quality or biological differences (e.g., tumour-infiltrating T cell abundance, malignant cells). Receptor count per sample gives a sense of diversity captured and can flag technical dropouts or high expansion. Fewer unique receptors relative to the number of cells can indicate greater clonal expansion. It is useful to investigate the biological and technical factors behind this pattern.

R 
idata_stats <- airr_desc_chains(idata)

idata_stats

*             <int>      <int>       <int> <chr>    <int> <chr> 
1                 3       6775        3495 TRB       6775 Tumor 
2                 1       3820        3721 TRB       3820 Blood 
3                 2       5956        2672 TRB       5956 Normal

The plot shows the number of unique receptors against the number of barcodes. The dashed lines indicate the ratio between them. Repertoires on the 100% line have one unique receptor per barcode. Those on the 50% line have, on average, two barcodes per unique receptor.

This plot shows one aggregated repertoire per tissue. To examine statistics for individual cell clusters, we first need to redefine the repertoires.

docs.title: 1b. Number of receptors and barcodes for cell clusters
docs.text:
The basic sample-level view is barely useful, and often you want to see how immune repertoires are distributed within cell subpopulations, e.g., by T cell cluster. With single-cell data, this is straightforward thanks to the flexible annotation model in immundata.

Currently, the idata object holds three repertoires, one for each tissue. Let's check that:

docs.title: 2a. Global gene usage
docs.text:
One of the most informative immune repertoire features is V(D)J gene segment usage. Shifts in gene usage can reveal biological signatures (e.g., enrichment of certain V genes in tumor-infiltrating clones), technical artifacts, or repertoire biases. Let's create a heatmap showing the frequency of each V gene segment across all cluster-tissue combinations. This gives a compact, bird's-eye view of usage patterns and potential "hotspots" of expansion.

R 
gene_usage_full <- airr_desc_genes(
  idata,
  gene_col = "v_call",
  level    = "receptor"
)

gene_usage_full |> vis(col = c("Cluster", "Tissue"))

docs.title: 2b. Most overrepresented V gene segments
docs.text:
The full overview can be difficult to interpret. Let's focus on the strongest signals: which V genes are most common across samples and repertoires? This can help reveal outlier samples or overall biases.

R 
# Compute V gene usage for all repertoires (by receptor count, split by tissue if present)
gene_usage_full <- airr_desc_genes(
  idata,
  gene_col = "v_call",
  level    = "receptor"
)

top_n <- 10

top_vgenes <- gene_usage_full |> 
  group_by(Tissue, v_call) |> 
  summarize(n = sum(n), .groups = "drop") |> 
  group_by(Tissue) |> 
  slice_max(order_by = n, n = top_n) |> 
  ungroup()

# Collect the *union* of all top genes across tissues
top_gene_set <- unique(top_vgenes$v_call)

# Filter to only these V genes for the heatmap (across all clusters and tissues)
usage_focus <- gene_usage_full |> 
  filter(v_call %in% top_gene_set)

usage_focus |> vis(col = c("Cluster", "Tissue"))

docs.title: 2c. Cluster-specific V gene distribution
docs.text:
We can use the same approach to focus on specific clusters of interest:

R 
# We use special functions from duckdb to filter clusters of interest
gene_usage_full <- idata |> 
  filter_immundata(dd$regexp_matches(Cluster, "Treg|Trm")) |> 
  airr_desc_genes(
    gene_col = "v_call",
    level    = "receptor"
  )

top_n <- 10

top_vgenes <- gene_usage_full |> 
  group_by(Tissue, v_call) |> 
  summarize(n = sum(n), .groups = "drop") |> 
  group_by(Tissue) |> 
  slice_max(order_by = n, n = top_n) |> 
  ungroup()

# Collect the *union* of all top genes across tissues
top_gene_set <- unique(top_vgenes$v_call)

# Filter to only these V genes for the heatmap (across all clusters and tissues)
usage_focus <- gene_usage_full |> 
  filter(v_call %in% top_gene_set)

usage_focus |> vis(col = c("Cluster", "Tissue"))

  • The rows are the most frequent V genes (union of top N per tissue).

  • The columns represent every observed (Cluster, Tissue) combination.

  • Color shows how often each V gene appears in each group.

docs.title: 3a. CDR3 length distribution for the full dataset
docs.text:
The CDR3 length distribution is a key QC and biological fingerprint of an immune repertoire. It can reveal technical artifacts (e.g., primer/UMI bias), repertoire selection, or expansion of unusual clones in disease states.

We can compute and visualize CDR3 length distributions across all tissues and clusters.

R 
# Compute CDR3 length stats for all repertoires (default is cdr3_aa)
length_stats <- airr_desc_lengths(
  idata,
  seq_col = "cdr3"
)

length_stats |> vis(fill = "Tissue", facet = "Tissue")

docs.title: 3b. CDR3 length distribution for the selected clusters
docs.text:
You can also zoom in on clusters of interest (e.g., Trm, Treg) for fine-grained analysis.

R 
# Choose clusters to display
selected_clusters <- c("Trm", "Treg")

length_stats_sel <- length_stats %>%
  filter(grepl("Trm|Treg", Cluster))

ggplot(length_stats_sel, aes(x = seq_len, y = pct, color = Tissue)) +
  geom_line(stat = "identity", linewidth = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ Cluster, scales = "free_y") +
  ggtitle("CDR3 length distribution in Trm and Treg clusters") +
  xlab("CDR3 length (amino acids)") +
  ylab("% receptors") +
  ggsci::scale_color_locuszoom()

  • Possible interpretation:

  • Most TCR/BCR repertoires peak at 13--15 amino acids for CDR3, but expansions, artifacts, or certain subsets may show longer or shorter tails.

  • Comparing distributions across tissues/clusters can highlight biologically relevant skewing (e.g., enrichment of unusually long or short CDR3s in tumors).

docs.title: Clonality: quantifying immune expansion
docs.text:
Immune repertoires are rarely flat. Certain T or B cell receptors expand dramatically in response to infection, cancer, or autoimmunity. Quantifying clonality lets you:

  • Detect immune responses ("public" expansions or tumor-infiltrating clones)
  • Compare the expansion across samples, tissues, or cell states
  • Identify technical problems (e.g., overamplification)

Currently there are three ways to summarize clonality:

  1. airr_clonality_line Rank--abundance plots Shows how steep the line of receptor abundances is.
  2. airr_clonality_prop Clonal space partitions by proportion Shows how much space is occupied by hyperexpanded, large, or rare clones.
  3. airr_clonality_rank Clonal space partitions by rank Shows how much space is occupied by receptors from different bins: the 10 most abundant receptors, the 100 most abundant receptors, etc.

Note: These functions calculate repertoire-level statistics. To label individual receptors by clonality, e.g., to highlight hyperexpanded receptors on a UMAP, use the annotate_clonality_*() functions. We'll return to these in the sections below.

docs.title: 1. Rank abundance
docs.text:
A rank abundance plot shows, for each sample (or group), how cell counts drop as you go from the most to least abundant clone. In other words, how steep the clonal hierarchy is.

  • Steep curves: few highly expanded clones dominate (e.g., tumor or antigen-driven response)
  • Flat curves: repertoire is diverse and even
R 
# Compute the abundance (cell/UMI count) for top 1000 clones per repertoire
clonal_line <- airr_clonality_line(
  idata,
  limit = 1000
)
clonal_line

docs.title: 2. Clonal space partitioning
docs.text:
Sometimes, you want to summarize clonal expansion in a single barplot splitting each repertoire into bins by abundance. For example:

  • "Hyperexpanded": clones with ≥1% of all cells
  • "Large": ≥0.1%, etc.
  • "Rare": all the way down to singletons

This lets you compare how much of each tissue or cluster is occupied by hyperexpanded, large, small and rare clones.

  • When using clusters or annotations, make sure you have enough cells per group for the statistics to be meaningful.

docs.title: Diversity: how rich and even are your repertoires?
docs.text:
True immune diversity is about more than just the number of unique sequences. It's about the balance of clone sizes and the richness of the repertoire - whether a handful of clones dominate or if the population is broad and even. Measuring diversity helps you:

  • Compare immune health or perturbation across tissues, patients, or clusters
  • Spot narrowing (loss of diversity) in disease, aging, or after therapy
  • Select features for machine learning and biomarker discovery

Diversity is the flip side of clonality:

  • Clonality highlights enrichment --- how much your repertoire is dominated by overexpanded ("clonal") receptors.
  • Diversity measures the overall heterogeneity and evenness of the repertoire --- are many clones present, and are they well balanced, or is the repertoire narrow?

In practical terms:

  • High diversity = many unique clones with relatively similar abundances. Typical of healthy, naive, or unperturbed immunity.
  • Low diversity = few clones dominate (high clonality). Often seen in strong immune responses, cancer, infection, or technical issues.

immunarch provides multiple diversity estimators, each with its own interpretation. To see all options or details, run ?airr_diversity in your R console. Supported methods are:

  1. airr_diversity_dxx() Coverage diversity --- D50, D20, D80... "How many top clones do you need to cover X% of all cells?" Small D50 = a few clones dominate (low diversity); large D50 = highly polyclonal.

  2. airr_diversity_chao1() A nonparametric asymptotic estimator of species richness (number of species in a population). One of the most used methods for estimating immune repertoire diversity.

  3. airr_diversity_shannon() Shannon entropy --- a gold standard, evenness-aware metric for diversity. Higher values = more diverse and even repertoire.

  4. airr_diversity_pielou() Pielou's evenness --- entropy normalized by clone count, ranges [0, 1]. Use when comparing repertoires of very different sizes.

  5. airr_diversity_index() Hill number (q=1) --- the "effective number" of clones, combines richness and evenness. Intuitive and robust: "How many equally frequent clones would give this entropy?"

  6. airr_diversity_hill() Hill diversity profile (q=0,1,2, ...) Powerful for exploring sensitivity to rare vs. abundant clones.

    • q=0: just unique count ("richness")
    • q=1: entropy-based (exp(Shannon))
    • q=2: Simpson's index (abundant clones dominate)
R 
# 1. Coverage diversity — D50: how many clones cover 50% of the repertoire?
d50 <- airr_diversity_dxx(idata, perc = 50)
p1 <- d50 |> vis()

# 3. Chao1 — non-parametric estimator of species richness (number of unique receptors)
chao <- airr_diversity_chao1(idata)
p2 <- chao |> vis(fill = "Tissue")

# 3. Shannon entropy — classical diversity (higher = more even)
shannon <- airr_diversity_shannon(idata)
p3 <- shannon |> vis(xval = "Cluster")

# 4. Pielou's evenness (normalized entropy, 0 = dominated, 1 = perfectly even)
pielou <- airr_diversity_pielou(idata)
p4 <- pielou |> vis(xval = "Tissue")
p5 <- pielou |> vis(facet = "Tissue", fill = "Cluster", dir = "v")

# 5. Hill number (q=1): the “effective number of clones”
hill1 <- airr_diversity_index(idata)

# 6. Hill diversity profile (q=0, 1, 2, ...)
hill_profile <- airr_diversity_hill(idata, q = c(0, 1, 2))

p1


p2


p3


p4


p5

docs.title: Rarefaction analysis
docs.text:
The three tissues were sampled at different depths. Before interpreting their diversity, we will inspect richness as a function of the number of retained T cells and repeat a comparison at a common cell count. In other words, we will explore how sampling depth affects diversity.

We create a tissue-level object for the following examples. The original idata still contains the tissue-by-cluster repertoires defined earlier. Here, counts and proportions refer to all retained TRB-bearing cells in each tissue, and receptor identity remains CDR3 amino-acid sequence plus V gene.

R 
idata_tissue <- agg_repertoires(idata, "Tissue")
idata_tissue$repertoires
## # A tibble: 3 × 4
##   imd_repertoire_id Tissue n_barcodes n_receptors
##               <int> <chr>       <dbl>       <int>
## 1                 1 Blood        3820        3721
## 2                 2 Normal       5956        2672
## 3                 3 Tumor        6775        3495

airr_diversity_rarefaction() estimates how many distinct receptors would be observed at each sampling depth. We use absolute cell counts and richness (norm = FALSE) and disable extrapolation, so every curve stays within that tissue's observed sampling depth. The ribbons summarize uncertainty under the estimator's bootstrap model.

R 
set.seed(42)

tissue_rarefaction <- airr_diversity_rarefaction(
  idata_tissue,
  norm = FALSE,
  extrapolation = 0,
  nboot = 50,
  verbose = FALSE
)

vis(tissue_rarefaction, color = "Tissue") +
  labs(x = "Retained cells sampled", y = "Expected distinct receptors")

Compare curves at the same cell count, rather than comparing only their final points. A rising curve indicates that more sampling is expected to reveal more receptors.

docs.title: Repeat the comparison at a common cell count
docs.text:
downsample_immundata() samples whole cells without replacement and returns a new ImmunData.

R 
common_depth <- min(idata_tissue$repertoires$n_barcodes)
idata_equal_depth <- downsample_immundata(
  idata_tissue, n = common_depth, seed = 42
)
idata_equal_depth$repertoires
## # A tibble: 3 × 4
##   imd_repertoire_id Tissue n_barcodes n_receptors
##               <int> <chr>       <dbl>       <int>
## 1                 1 Blood        3820        3721
## 2                 2 Normal       3820        1863
## 3                 3 Tumor        3820        2246

shannon_depth <- bind_rows(
  airr_diversity_shannon(idata_tissue) |> mutate(Depth = "Observed"),
  airr_diversity_shannon(idata_equal_depth) |> mutate(Depth = "Equal cell count")
)

ggplot(shannon_depth, aes(x = Tissue, y = shannon, fill = Depth)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(x = "Tissue", y = "Shannon entropy (bits)", fill = "Sampling depth")

This is one reproducible sensitivity check. For a substantive comparison, repeat downsampling with several seeds and examine whether the conclusion persists. Equal cell counts do not correct differences in cell capture or replace independent biological replicates. We will continue the receptor-selection examples with idata_tissue in the section after the next one.

We can now calculate statistics for individual repertoires. But how similar are the repertoires to one another? In the next section, we'll compare them using their receptor features.

docs.title: Quantify repertoire similarity
docs.text:
In immunology, public receptors are TCRs or BCRs that appear in multiple individuals or samples, suggesting convergent responses to shared antigens, or technical "publicity" due to biases. Measuring the overlap between repertoires helps you:

  • Check for a signal of shared, or "public," immune receptors.
  • QC for sample swap, cross-contamination, or replicate similarity
  • Compare cohort similarity or donor-sharing at scale

immunarch provides the following functions for quantifying this:

  • repsim_intersection() Intersection: how many receptor identities were observed in both tissues? Use for overlap heatmaps, or to check how much two samples have in common.

  • repsim_jaccard() Jaccard similarity: what fraction of the combined set of observed identities is shared? (⁠|A∩B| / |A∪B|⁠). This normalizes for differences in sample size---great for comparing across experiments or donors.

  • repsim_chao_jaccard() Chao-Jaccard similarity: how similar are the repertoires after estimating the contribution of shared receptors missed through limited sampling? Accounts for the sampling randomness.

  • repsim_morisita_horn() Morisita-Horn similarity: do the same receptors account for much of the cell abundance in both tissues? Dominant public immune receptors have more influence on this score.

  • repsim_bray() Bray-Curtis similarity: how much of the receptor abundance composition is shared between tissues? Resembles the Morisita-Horn index, more sensitive to the sampling size differences, but gives less weight to extremes and more weight to the rare immune receptors. Good middle ground.

For full options and details, run ?repsim in your R console.

R 
repsim_intersection(idata_tissue) |> vis()


repsim_jaccard(idata_tissue) |> vis()


repsim_chao_jaccard(idata_tissue) |> vis()


repsim_morisita_horn(idata_tissue) |> vis()


repsim_bray(idata_tissue) |> vis()

To examine whether the comparison depends on the largest expansions, repeat Bray-Curtis with transform = "log1p". This exploratory transformation changes the abundance scale, so interpret the score as similarity on that transformed scale rather than a fraction of original cell abundance.

R 
repsim_bray(idata_tissue, transform = "log1p") |> vis()

We can also inspect the original proportions of individual receptors shared by blood and tumour. Each point in this plot is a shared receptor identity.

R 
vis(idata_tissue, x = "Blood", y = "Tumor", lm = FALSE)

We found receptors shared between repertoires. Which receptors are they, and how can we investigate them? In the next section, we'll extract, analyse and visualise them.

docs.title: Discover and annotate immune receptors
docs.text: This section was written quickly to cover a frequently requested feature. A more polished version will be available in a future release.

docs.title: Track expanded tumour receptors across tissues
docs.text:
Which receptors dominate the tumour, and are they also detected in blood or normal adjacent tissue? We select receptors that each account for at least 1% of the retained tumour cells, then follow those identities in all three tissues.

R 
tumour_id <- idata_tissue$repertoires |>
  filter(Tissue == "Tumor") |>
  pull(imd_repertoire_id)

tumour_source <- filter(
  idata_tissue,
  Tissue == "Tumor", 
  imd_proportion >= 0.01
)
tracked_tumour <- vdj_track(
  idata_tissue,
  from = tumour_source,
  output = "df"
)
tracked_tumour$Tissue <- factor(
  tracked_tumour$Tissue, levels = c("Blood", "Normal", "Tumor")
)

vis(tracked_tumour, xval = "Tissue", plot = "line")


vis(tracked_tumour, xval = "Tissue", plot = "line", yval = "imd_orig_count")

The summary has one row per selected receptor and tissue, including zeros where the receptor was unobserved. Columns imd_orig_count and imd_orig_proportion preserve the abundances in the original tissue repertoires. In particular, the plotted proportions are not renormalized to sum to one over the selected receptors.

For a stacked view, use plot = "area":

R 
vis(tracked_tumour, xval = "Tissue", plot = "area")

An alluvial view is available with the optional ggalluvial package. Install it once with install.packages("ggalluvial"), then plot:

R 
vis(tracked_tumour, xval = "Tissue", plot = "alluvial")

docs.title: Find the tumour clusters carrying these receptors
docs.text:
Which tumour cell clusters contain the most cells carrying our two expanded receptors? idata already has tissue-by-cluster repertoires, so we only need to filter for tumour cells and pass the same tumour_source to vdj_track().

R 
tumour_clusters <- filter(idata, Tissue == "Tumor", !is.na(Cluster))
tracked_clusters <- vdj_track(tumour_clusters,
  from = tumour_source, output = "df")

vis(tracked_clusters, xval = "Cluster", plot = "line",
  yval = "imd_orig_count", title = "Tumour-expanded receptors by cell cluster") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

To inspect the peaks, list the three clusters containing the most cells for each receptor. The percentage is relative to all retained TRB-bearing cells in that cluster, so it also helps compare clusters of different sizes.

R 
cluster_peaks <- tracked_clusters |>
  filter(imd_orig_count > 0) |>
  slice_max(imd_orig_count, n = 3, by = c(cdr3, v_call), with_ties = FALSE) |>

docs.text:
Build a compact panel of the selected CDR3--V combinations and annotate the full tissue object.

R 
tumour_panel <- tracked_tumour |>
  distinct(cdr3, v_call) |>
  duckplyr::as_duckdb_tibble() |>
  mutate(tumour_receptor_group = "Expanded tumour receptor")

idata_tumour_marked <- annotate_with_database(
  idata_tissue,
  db = tumour_panel,
  by = c(cdr3 = "cdr3", v_call = "v_call"),
  label_col = "tumour_receptor_group"
) |>
  mutate(tumour_receptor_group = coalesce(
    tumour_receptor_group, "Other retained TRB"
  ))

sdata_tumour <- annotate_seurat(
  idata_tumour_marked, sdata, cols = "tumour_receptor_group"
)
sdata_tumour$tumour_receptor_group[
  is.na(sdata_tumour$tumour_receptor_group)
] <- "No retained TRB"

DimPlot(sdata_tumour, reduction = "umap",
  group.by = "tumour_receptor_group", order = "Expanded tumour receptor",
  cols = c("Expanded tumour receptor" = "#1E40AF",
    "Other retained TRB" = "#D8B365", "No retained TRB" = "#8C8C8C"))

The labels distinguish cells carrying a selected receptor, other cells with a retained TRB, and transcriptomic cells without a retained TRB in this analysis. Blue marks the selected receptors, tan marks other retained TRBs, and grey marks cells without a retained TRB.

docs.title: Select shared and tissue-restricted receptors
docs.text:
annotate_public() adds sharing statistics while retaining the full object. With one repertoire per tissue, imd_public_incidence is the number of tissues in which a receptor was observed. We can transfer this label to Seurat using the same barcode interface as for clonality annotations (see below).

R 
idata_tissue_public <- annotate_public(idata_tissue)
## No strata found in idata$repertoires. Computing global publicness metrics only.
## Run `immundata::agg_strata()` to add per-strata metrics.
sdata_public <- annotate_seurat(
  idata_tissue_public, sdata, cols = "imd_public_incidence"
)
sdata_public$tissue_sharing <- ifelse(
  is.na(sdata_public$imd_public_incidence), "No retained TRB",
  paste0("Observed in ", sdata_public$imd_public_incidence, " tissue(s)")
)
DimPlot(sdata_public, reduction = "umap",
  group.by = "tissue_sharing", shuffle = TRUE)

docs.title: Summarize receptor sharing directly
docs.text:
The receptor-level summary complements the cell-level UMAP. Pass the annotated object to vis() to count distinct receptor identities by the number of repertoires in which they were detected. Reusing idata_tissue_public avoids recomputing the annotations, or you can use annotate_public(idata_tissue) |> vis(plot = "incidence").

R 
idata_tissue_public |> vis(plot = "incidence")

Each receptor contributes once to this histogram, regardless of how many cells carry it. Here there is one repertoire per tissue, so incidence counts tissues.

docs.title: Show the density of cells carrying shared receptors
docs.text:
We can also draw density contours for cells whose receptor was detected in at least two tissues. We use Seurat metadata and UMAP coordinates already held in memory; repertoire calculations remain in ImmunData.

R 
sharing_umap <- FetchData(sdata_public,
  vars = c("UMAP_1", "UMAP_2", "imd_public_incidence"), clean = FALSE)
shared_umap <- sharing_umap |>
  filter(!is.na(imd_public_incidence), imd_public_incidence >= 2)

ggplot(sharing_umap, aes(x = UMAP_1, y = UMAP_2)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey85", size = 0.2) +
  geom_density_2d(data = shared_umap, colour = "#0072B2",
    linewidth = 0.6, bins = 6) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Density of cells carrying shared receptors",
    subtitle = "Receptors detected in at least two tissues",
    x = "UMAP 1", y = "UMAP 2")

The density contours show where those cells concentrate on the displayed UMAP. They depend on sampling and the embedding, and do not measure gene expression or establish enrichment relative to the surrounding cells. Use the colouring plot to inspect the individual cells and their sharing labels.

vdj_public() selects receptor identities according to explicit rules. Every rule in one call is evaluated against the original input, and all rules must pass. Here we require observation in both tumour and blood, then retain those identities wherever they occur, including normal tissue.

R 
blood_id <- idata_tissue$repertoires |>
  filter(Tissue == "Blood") |>
  pull(imd_repertoire_id)

shared_tumour_blood <- vdj_public(
  idata_tissue,
  make_public_filter(repertoires = tumour_id, min_incidence = 1L),
  make_public_filter(repertoires = blood_id, min_incidence = 1L)
)

vis(shared_tumour_blood, plot = "public", reference = idata_tissue,
  xval = "Tissue", fill = "Tissue")

Bars show the fraction of original tissue cell abundance carried by the selected receptors. Dots show how many of the selected receptor identities were detected in each tissue, divided by the size of the selected identity set. These are different denominators: a few expanded receptors can occupy much of a tissue's cell abundance even when only a small fraction of the selected identities is detected there.

To find tumour-restricted candidates, require an observed tumour proportion of at least 0.1% and no observations in blood or normal tissue:

other_tissue_ids <- idata_tissue$repertoires |>
  filter(Tissue != "Tumor") |>
  pull(imd_repertoire_id)

tumour_restricted <- vdj_public(
  idata_tissue,
  make_public_filter(repertoires = tumour_id,
    min_proportion = 0.001, min_incidence = 1L),
  make_public_filter(repertoires = other_tissue_ids, max_incidence = 0L)
)

docs.title: Annotate CMV-associated sequences from VDJdb
docs.text: This workflow has three steps: prepare a reference panel, annotate our receptors, then track and visualize the matches. We use human TRB records associated with CMV from the pinned VDJdb 2026-06-03 release.

docs.title: Load the reference panel
docs.text:
Download the archive once through BiocFileCache and extract its slim table. Subsequent runs reuse the cached download.

R 
vdjdb_zip <- BiocFileCache::bfcrpath(
  BiocFileCache::BiocFileCache(ask = FALSE),
  "https://github.com/antigenomics/vdjdb-db/releases/download/2026-06-03/vdjdb-2026-06-03.zip"
)
utils::unzip(vdjdb_zip, files = "vdjdb-2026-06-03/vdjdb.slim.txt", exdir = tempdir())
vdjdb <- duckplyr::read_csv_duckdb(
  file.path(tempdir(), "vdjdb-2026-06-03/vdjdb.slim.txt"),
  options = list(delim = "\t", max_line_size = 10000000)
)

cmv_panel <- vdjdb |>
  filter(species == "HomoSapiens", gene == "TRB",
    antigen.species == "CMV", vdjdb.score > 0) |>
  distinct(cdr3, gene) |>
  mutate(cmv_db_match = TRUE) |>
  compute()

We keep positive-score records and one row per CDR3--locus combination. This makes the panel a simple yes/no annotation and prevents repeated database records from duplicating our cells.

docs.title: Annotate and inspect the matches
docs.text:
annotate_with_database() adds the match label to ImmunData. We then select the labelled receptors and ask vdj_track() for their abundances in the original tissue repertoires.

R 
idata_cmv <- annotate_with_database(
  idata_tissue, db = cmv_panel,
  by = c(cdr3 = "cdr3", locus = "gene"), label_col = "cmv_db_match"
)
cmv_receptors <- filter(idata_cmv, cmv_db_match)
cmv_tracking <- vdj_track(idata_tissue, from = cmv_receptors, output = "df")

cmv_matches <- cmv_tracking |>
  filter(imd_orig_count > 0) |>
  select(Tissue, cdr3, v_call, imd_orig_count)
knitr::kable(cmv_matches,
  col.names = c("Tissue", "CDR3 amino acids", "V gene", "Cells"))
Tissue CDR3 amino acids V gene Cells Blood CASSLGQGNSPLHF TRBV5-6 1 Blood CASSLGTGELFF TRBV11-2 1 Tumor CASSPGQLQETQYF TRBV7-8 1 Tumor CASSRLAGGTGELFF TRBV5-6 1 Tumor CASSAGDEQYF TRBV18 1 Tumor CASSPGDEQFF TRBV6-6 1

The table shows 6 detected receptor--tissue combinations, carried by 6 cells. Matching uses CDR3 and locus, while our receptor identities still include the V gene.

docs.title: Highlight the matched cells and follow their abundances
docs.text:
Transfer the match label to Seurat and highlight the matching cells. Large red points make these rare matches visible against the grey background.

R 
sdata_cmv <- annotate_seurat(idata_cmv, sdata, cols = "cmv_db_match")
sdata_cmv$cmv_db_match <- sdata_cmv$cmv_db_match %in% TRUE
cmv_cells <- WhichCells(sdata_cmv, expression = cmv_db_match %in% TRUE)
DimPlot(sdata_cmv, reduction = "umap",
  cells.highlight = list("CMV-panel match" = cmv_cells),
  cols = "grey85", cols.highlight = "#D73027",
  pt.size = 0.15, sizes.highlight = 2.5)

There are 4 matched cells in this Seurat object. Matched VDJ cells absent from the transcriptomic object cannot appear on its UMAP.

Plot the same receptors across tissues with vis(). Counts and proportions refer to the original tissue repertoires, including zero where unobserved.

R 
vis(cmv_tracking, xval = "Tissue", plot = "line")

docs.title: Annotating receptors by clonality
docs.text:
Clonality tells us how overabundant a receptor is inside a repertoire. Here we add a label per receptor, then pass a single label per cell to Seurat for easy plotting on UMAP.

You can choose one of two simple rules:

  • By proportion (recommended to start): bins like Hyperexpanded, Large, ... based on the receptor's proportion within the repertoire.
  • By rank: bins by the receptor's rank (top 10, top 100, ...) within the repertoire.

Both helpers keep your data intact and add new columns to ImmunData.

Note: Thresholds are heuristics. They are good defaults, but are not universal truths. You have been warned.

R 
idata <- annotate_clonality_prop(idata)

sdata <- annotate_seurat(idata, sdata, cols = "clonal_prop_bin")

Seurat::DimPlot(sdata, reduction = "umap", group.by = "clonal_prop_bin", shuffle = TRUE)


idata <- annotate_clonality_rank(idata)

sdata <- annotate_seurat(idata, sdata, cols = "clonal_rank_bin")

Seurat::DimPlot(sdata, reduction = "umap", group.by = "clonal_rank_bin", shuffle = TRUE)

docs.title: Appendix A: Function naming schema
docs.text:
immunarch follows a specific naming scheme to distinguish between output types of the different functions and clearly split the functions to different domains of AIRR data analysis. In other words, just by looking at the function name, you can infer two things:

  • what to expect as an output from this function

  • to what domain of data analysis it belongs, e.g., diversity, Ig analysis, etc.

A positive consequence of having functions splitted to large domains or "function families" is to have documentation for one function family in one place. E.g., you can run ?airr_desc to get help for all functions in the family of descriptive statistics functions. Same for ?annotate_clonality and others.

Exploratory data analysis functions:

  • airr_* functions work on the repertoire-level (hence "AIRR") and compute per-repertoire descriptive statistics. They return repertoire-level statistics --- a table with per-repertoire computed statistics and joined metadata for the downstream analysis and visualisation convenience.

  • annotate_* functions work on the receptor-level and return the input ImmunDatas but with new columns added. Because ImmunData is immutable data structure, strictly speaking, you always get a new ImmunData with additional annotation columns added, but with the same receptor structure and counts, but you can think that this is the very same object you passed to the function as an input.

  • repsim_* functions work on the inter-repertoire level and return similarity or distance matrices depending on the method used. E.g., a matrix with pairwise Jaccard similarities.

  • vdj_* functions work on the receptor-level. They analyse immune receptors and return a new ImmunData following the function logic. The output is usually a completely new and smaller ImmunData, e.g., with public receptors or receptors, found in an immunogenicity database. Optionally, they can return a data frame for faster visualisation and analysis, although you need to make sure your RAM can handle it.

[!NOTE] Q: Why is it different in R and Python? Why can't we have clonality_annotate in R or annotate_clonality in Python?

A: This is an opinionated decision made to emulate the modules of Python in R. There is no system of modules in R, so to ensure more convenient user experience, I provide functions in this way to minimize the amount of scope names to remember. There are almost 10 diversity metrics alone, and remembering all of this could be quite cumbersome. Instead, a user can always press "tab" to autocomplete function names from airr_diversity_*. In Python, the reasoning is different. Due to the modular structure of packages, it is easier to split the scope into different domains, e.g., immunarch.clonality or immunarch.public, so the necessary scopes could be imported to the workspace. Hence the Python users look for modules with a specific scope first, and export necessary methods.

docs.title: 聚合：定义受体（receptors）与受体库（repertoires）
docs.text:
第二个关键概念是如何定义什么是受体和受体库。当你的数据来自像 Cell Ranger 这样的 AIRR 组装工具时，你会得到许多独立的 V(D)J 链（chains）。 但大多数问题是关于受体（receptors）（例如，“筛选供体 A 在第 30 天的所有受体”）或受体库（repertoires）（例如，“免疫治疗应答者与非应答者在基因使用方面有什么差异？”）。

换句话说，这个概念背后的假设是：研究者在链（重排）层面工作，但在受体与受体库层面思考。immundata 通过受控聚合（controlled aggregation）帮助你从原始链跃迁到这些更高层次的对象。也就是说，你先制定清晰的规则来说明如何把链合成为受体、再把受体合成为受体库，软件会据此执行。

docs.title: agg_receptors(): 定义“一个受体”的含义
docs.text:
使用 immundata::agg_receptors() 来决定在你的研究中如何构建受体，即在你的研究中一个受体意味着什么。

  1. 先选择一个schema（配方）。例如：
  2. 不带 V 基因片段的单链。
  3. 带 V 基因片段的单链。
  4. 将共享同一条形码且具有 α 与 β 位点的链配对。
  5. 将每个 IGH 与具有相同 CDR3 氨基酸序列的 IGL 进行匹配。
  6. 该函数会重建或重新聚合数据并返回一个新的 ImmunData 对象。底层数据不会被修改；你只是获得了一个数据的新“视图”。
  7. 每个受体都会得到一个稳定的 ID，并保留到其原始链与条形码的链接。
  8. 如果你之后更改了受体定义，只需重新运行此步骤即可。无需编辑基于该特定受体定义构建的其余流程。

docs.title: agg_repertoires(): 将受体分组成有意义的集合
docs.text:
使用 immundata::agg_repertoires() 来声明应如何把受体分组成用于分析的受体库（repertoires）。

  • 组例：来自某一次活检的所有受体、治疗应答者的所有受体、某单细胞簇中的受体，或任意元数据列的组合。
  • 结果是在物理表 idata$repertoires 中得到基本计数（链、条形码、唯一受体）。每个受体库都保留与其所含受体的直接链接。因此，同样，底层数据并未改变——只是其上方的轻量注释。

docs.title: 为什么这种设计有帮助
docs.text:
• 简单而精确： 你可以计算度量（如 Jaccard 相似度、多样性等），而且精确的受体定义（例如 "cdr3+v"）会和结果一起保存，这样你可以清楚追溯当前 ImmunData 是在何种定义下构建的。这减少了人为失误，因为每次计算时你不需要重复输入相同的受体 schema（如 "cdr3+v"）。

  • 内置完整的数据沿袭（data lineage）：

  • 每个受体知道自己包含哪些链。

  • 每个受体库知道自己包含哪些受体。
  • 完整的“配方”保存在 ImmunData 对象的元数据中。 六个月之后——或六位审稿人之后——你都能把任一汇总统计追溯到产生它的精确链，实现完全可复现、无隐性变换的分析流程。

docs.title: 单位：链（chain）→ 条形码（barcode）→ 受体（receptor）
docs.text:
第一个关键概念是数据操作的基本单位，包括：

  • 链（Chain）是一条 V(D)J 序列记录（read/contig/分子），例如带有 V(D)J 基因及其他信息（包括基因表达与免疫原性）的 TRA、TRB、IGH 或 IGL。它是最小的数据单位，是一切的基石。数据导入（ingest）后保持不变，因此你可以随时下钻到其精确的核苷酸/氨基酸序列及注释。

  • 条形码（Barcode）是一个物理容器，可包含 0、1 或多条链。

  • 单细胞：一个液滴/细胞条形码。

  • 空间转录组：一个点位（spot）条形码（可能捕获来自多个细胞的转录本）。
  • 批量测序（Bulk）：不使用“barcode”这个术语，实质上把每条链都视作独立的“条形码”。

它是“存放”相关生物学数据的生物学单位，用于对相同的链进行聚合，并统计来自不同条形码的同一受体的计数。

  • 受体（Receptor）是链的逻辑分组，代表一个用于下游分析与报告的生物学受体实例。所有免疫受体库统计或受体追踪都在受体层面计算。受体由用户指定的受体模式（schema）定义，包含：

  • 受体特征：通常为 CDR3 氨基酸（AA）序列，可选地与 V 基因（以及需要时的 J 基因或长度）组合。

  • 受体链：例如单链、α+β（TCR）、重链+轻链（BCR），或其他明确定义的组合。在多链情形（如双 α）中，需要明确你的配对/合并规则。

总结：immundata 以链存储信息，条形码把多条链打包在一起，而受体是进行受体库统计的最小单位。

术语 通俗解释 immundata 中的表示 角色 Chain（链） 来自一次 read 或 contig 的单条 V(D)J 转录本（如 TRA 或 IGH）。 物理表 idata$annotations 中的一行；保留 locus、cdr3、umis/reads 及其他关键重排特征。 原始数据单位——原子级构件。 Barcode / Cell 捕获该链的液滴（10x）、点位（Visium）或孔板孔。 列 imd_barcode。 物理集合——将共享同一捕获隔间的链分组。 Receptor（受体） 你要分析的生物学受体：来自同一细胞的一条单链 或 一对（αβ、重-轻）链。 虚拟表 idata$receptors；唯一 ID imd_receptor_id。 逻辑单位——AIRR 统计的最小对象。 Repertoire 按样本、供体、细胞簇等分组的一组受体。 物理表 idata$repertoires；唯一 ID imd_repertoire_id；包含你选择的分组列。 聚合单位——用于比较分析的更高层级分组。

docs.title: 基于流水线的执行：不可变性与物化（materialization）
docs.text:
在前两个概念中我们多次谈到数据可追溯性（data lineage）。但只有当工作流程中的每一步都可被重新执行时，数据沿袭才有意义——换句话说，即可复现。要让结果可复现，每个分析步骤都必须能在不改变底层数据（无副作用）的情况下被轻松重跑。 在由 immundata 驱动的管线中，一次分析是由不可变（immutable）的转换构成的流水线：

  • 每个函数都会返回一个全新的 ImmunData 对象。
  • 底层数据不被修改。新对象 = 数据的新视图。
  • 这一串 ImmunData 对象记录了数据如何从原始链（chains）走到最终数字。

docs.title: 默认落盘，按需入内存
docs.text:
不可变性乍看并不方便，但它使我们能够处理大于内存（larger-than-RAM）的免疫受体数据集。immundata 使用了多种聪明的数据工程技巧：

  • 免疫数据表以 Parquet 文件落盘（列式压缩格式，加速数据分析）。
  • 只有在计算需要时才将数据物化（即加载到内存）。例如做子集或输出最终指标（如重叠指数）。
  • 对于中等规模数据（如 ~10 GB），这几乎是“无感”的：immundata 使用的轻量数据库 DuckDB 会从文件流式读取，并给你一个常规的内存数据框。
  • 而对大型数据（如 ~100 GB），同一套代码依然有效，因为 Parquet 与数据视图的组合让 DuckDB 能高效查询底层数据，避免把无关部分装入内存。

权衡很清楚：要么像典型数据框那样全部在内存中工作（内存成为瓶颈）；要么构建不可变的转换，让 DuckDB 优化处理查询，从而实现对超内存数据的支持。

docs.title: “流水线思维”在日常中的含义
docs.text:
以不可变流水线思考意味着两件事：

  • 创建快照（snapshot）： 当遇到昂贵步骤时，使用 immundata::write_immundata() 保存一个中间的 ImmunData 对象。该函数会生成一个新的 ImmunData，你随后就用这个新对象，获得大幅加速。示例：计算到某些模式或序列的编辑距离。如果在这一步后创建快照，这些距离会被落盘；如果不创建，之后每次在当前 ImmunData 上做转换或计算时，immundata 都得重新计算距离——而你知道距离计算有多耗时。
  • 默认假设可重跑： 任何人——同事，或未来的你在一台更强的机器上——都应该能从头到尾运行 pipeline.R 并得到完全一致的结果。

docs.title: 面向开发者：隐藏“水管”细节，把注意力还给生物学
docs.text:
基于 immundata 的包应当暴露简单而高层的函数，比如 compute_diversity() 或 plot_overlap()。 用户无需关心 ImmunData、DuckDB 或 Parquet。理想情况下，他们甚至察觉不到有一个落盘数据库的存在。

把数据工程留给数据工程师（和生物信息学家）。把注意力放在生物学上——那已经足够复杂了。

docs.title: Overview ZH
docs.text:
immundata splits the workflow into two clear phases:

  1. Ingestion – convert your AIRR files into a special format saved on disk, and then read them to a tidy immundata::ImmunData object

  2. Transformation – explore, annotate, filter and compute on that object

Before we go into more details for each of the phase, there are three straightforward yet essential immundata concepts to keep in mind. These concepts set it apart from data-frame-based AIRR libraries. By extension, the concepts affect how you would work with and even think about the data analysis in other packages such as immunarch which use immundata as a backbone for computations.

docs.title: 在 R 中将 immunarch::repLoad() 的输出转换为 ImmunData
docs.text:
用于将 immunarch v0.9 的受体库迁移为 immunarch 0.10/1.0 中的 ImmunData 数据集。

工作原理：

  • 接收一个 immunarch::repLoad() 对象（imm）。
  • 为每个受体库各写出一个 TSV（并添加文件名列）到 temp_folder。
  • 用 read_repertoires() 将这些 TSV 导入为 ImmunData。
  • 在 output_folder 下保存 Parquet 文件；返回一个 ImmunData 对象。

关键参数：

  • imm：immunarch::repLoad() 的输出。
  • output_folder：存放 Parquet 数据的位置（自动创建）。
  • schema：定义唯一受体键的字符向量 （默认 c("CDR3.aa", "V.name")；你也可以加入 "J.name"）。
  • temp_folder：写入中间 TSV 的位置（默认为临时目录）。
R 
library(immunarch)

# 1）加载 immunarch 对象（读取所有受体库 + 可选元数据）
immdata <- immunarch::repLoad("/path/to/your/files")

# 2）转换为 ImmunData（以 Parquet 为后端），必要时自定义受体键
idata <- from_immunarch(
  imm           = immdata,
  schema        = c("CDR3.aa", "V.name"),
  output_folder = "/path/to/immundata_out"
)

idata

可选地，你也可以在把对象传给 from_immunarch 之前，先在 immdata 中重命名列，使其更贴近 AIRR-C 格式：

R 
rename_to_airr <- function(df) {
  map <- c(
    "CDR3.aa"   = "cdr3_aa",
    "CDR3.nt"   = "cdr3_nt",
    "V.name"    = "v_call",
    "D.name"    = "d_call",
    "J.name"    = "j_call",
    "Clones"    = "umi_count",
    "Read.count"= "duplicate_count",
    "Barcode"   = "cell_id",
    "barcode"   = "cell_id",
    "Chain"     = "locus",
    "Gene"      = "locus",
    "Productive"= "productive"
  )

  present_old <- intersect(names(df), names(map))
  if (!length(present_old)) return(df)

  new_names <- unname(map[present_old])
  keep <- !duplicated(new_names)
  present_old <- present_old[keep]
  new_names    <- new_names[keep]

  spec <- stats::setNames(rlang::syms(present_old), new_names)
  dplyr::rename(df, !!!spec)
}

immdata$data <- lapply(immdata$data, rename_to_airr)

docs.title: 在 R 的 immunarch 中加载 AIRR-C 格式的批量测序免疫受体库数据
docs.text:
适用于批量 AIRR Rearrangement TSV（每行一个重排/受体）。前提：已安装 immunarch。

工作原理：

  • 从文件夹读取所有 AIRR-C TSV（批量模式）。
  • 将 AIRR 字段（如 v_call、j_call、junction_aa）映射到受体 schema。
  • 使用提供的计数字段设置受体丰度。

关键参数：

  • schema：你需要的特征（例如 junction_aa、v_call、j_call）
  • path：文件、通配符（glob）或包含文件的文件夹
  • count_col：通常是 umi_count 或 duplicate_count（若列名不同请相应调整）
R 
library(immunarch)

schema <- make_receptor_schema(features = c("junction_aa", "v_call"))
# 备选：
schema <- make_receptor_schema(features = c("cdr3_aa", "v_call"))

idata <- read_repertoires(
  path       = "/path/to/bulk_airr/*.tsv",
  schema     = schema,
  count_col  = "umi_count",
  preprocess = make_default_preprocessing("airr")
)

# 如果你有元数据，可以这样使用：
idata <- read_repertoires(
  path       = "/path/to/bulk_airr/*.tsv",
  metadata   = your_metadata_table,
  schema     = schema,
  count_col  = "umi_count",
  preprocess = make_default_preprocessing("airr")
)

# 如果你已经知道受体库（repertoire）schema：
idata <- read_repertoires(
  path              = "/path/to/bulk_airr/*.tsv",
  metadata          = your_metadata_table,
  schema            = schema,
  count_col         = "umi_count",
  preprocess        = make_default_preprocessing("airr"),
  repertoire_schema = c("Patient", "Cluster", "Response")
)

docs.title: 在 R 的 immunarch 中加载 AIRR-C 格式的单细胞测序免疫受体库数据
docs.text:
当你的单细胞数据导出为 AIRR-C，且包含细胞条形码与 locus 列时使用此方法。

工作原理：

  • 读取 AIRR-C TSV（每行一个 contig）。
  • 按条形码分组，并按 locus 配对（例如 TRA + TRB）。或仅选择指定的位点。
  • 使用 UMI/reads 列为每个位点选取排名最高的 contig（top contig）。

关键参数：

  • schema：你需要的特征（例如 junction_aa、v_call、j_call）
  • path：文件、通配符（glob）或包含文件的文件夹
  • barcode_col：包含条形码的列——cell_id
  • locus_col：包含位点信息的列——"locus"
  • umi_col：包含 UMI 信息的列，通常是 umi_count 或 duplicate_count
R 
library(immunarch)

# 如果你有两条链，可以只选择其中一条并过滤其他：
schema <- make_receptor_schema(features = c("junction_aa", "v_call"), chains = c("TCRA"))
# 或创建配对链受体：
schema <- make_receptor_schema(features = c("junction_aa", "v_call"), chains = c("TCRA", "TCRB"))

idata <- read_repertoires(
  path        = "/path/to/sc_airr/*.tsv",
  schema      = schema,
  barcode_col = "cell_id",
  locus_col   = "locus",
  umi_col     = "umi_count",
  preprocess  = make_default_preprocessing("airr")
)

# 如果你有元数据，可以这样使用：
idata <- read_repertoires(
  path        = "/path/to/sc_airr/*.tsv",
  schema      = schema,
  metadata    = your_metadata_table,
  barcode_col = "cell_id",
  locus_col   = "locus",
  umi_col     = "umi_count",
  preprocess  = make_default_preprocessing("airr")
)

# 如果你已经知道受体库（repertoire）schema：
idata <- read_repertoires(
  path              = "/path/to/sc_airr/*.tsv",
  schema            = schema,
  metadata          = your_metadata_table,
  barcode_col       = "cell_id",
  locus_col         = "locus",
  umi_col           = "umi_count",
  preprocess        = make_default_preprocessing("airr"),
  repertoire_schema = c("Patient", "Cluster", "Response")
)

docs.title: 快速上手（Quick Start）
docs.text: 五分钟导览：加载 immunarch，获取示例数据，运行核心分析，并使用随包提供的 immundata 工具摄取 AIRR 数据。

docs.title: 1) 加载工具包
docs.text:
R 
library(immunarch)

docs.title: 2) 获取示例数据并设置分组
docs.text:
R 
# 小型演示数据集
idata <- get_test_idata() |> agg_repertoires("Therapy")

# 打印精简摘要
idata

docs.title: 3) 初步分析（First-look analyses）
docs.text:
R 
# 基因使用（例如 V 基因）
airr_stats_genes(idata, gene_col = "v_call") |> vis()

# 公共性 / 重叠
airr_public_jaccard(idata) |> vis()

# 克隆性（丰度分箱）
airr_clonality_prop(idata)

# 多样性（均匀度）
airr_diversity_pielou(idata) |> vis()

docs.title: 4)（可选）按受体注释克隆性并在 Seurat 中绘图
docs.text:
R 
# 添加每受体的克隆性标签
idata <- annotate_clonality_prop(idata)

# 按条形码把标签拷贝到 Seurat 对象并给 UMAP 上色
#（假设你在流程早前已创建了 `sdata`）
sdata <- annotate_seurat(idata, sdata, cols = "clonal_prop_bin")
Seurat::DimPlot(sdata, reduction = "umap", group.by = "clonal_prop_bin", shuffle = TRUE)

docs.title: 5)（可选）使用随包的数据层摄取 AIRR 数据
docs.text:
immundata 与 immunarch 一起发布。你可以直接调用其读取函数以灵活导入。

R 
# 读取 AIRR TSV（示例）
md_path <- system.file("extdata/tsv", "metadata.tsv", package = "immundata")
files <- c(
    system.file("extdata/tsv", "sample_0_1k.tsv", package = "immundata"),
    system.file("extdata/tsv", "sample_1k_2k.tsv", package = "immundata")
)

md <- read_metadata(md_path)
idata <- read_repertoires(
path     = files,
schema   = c("cdr3_aa", "v_call"),
metadata = md
)

# 继续进行 immunarch 分析
idata |> agg_repertoires("Therapy") |> airr_clonality_prop()
